ancestry_summary.statement_nl: Let [m]_q = (1−q^m)/(1−q), let (a;q)_k = ∏_{j=0}^{k−1} (1−aq^j), let (a,b,c;q)_k = (a;q)_k (b;q)_k (c;q)_k, and let Φ_n(q) be the nth cyclotomic polynomial. Prove that for positive integers d and r with gcd(d,r)=1 and r ≤ d, and for every integer n > 1 with n ≡ 1 mod 2d, we have Σ_{k=0}^{n−1} [3dk+r]_q (q^r,q^r,q^d;q^{2d})_k (q^d;q^d)_k^2 q^(k(d−dk−2r)/2) / (q^{2d};q^{2d})_k ≡ [rn]_q q^(r(1−n)/2) mod [n]_q Φ_n(q)^2.

ancestry_summary.statement_nl: Let [m]_q = (1−q^m)/(1−q), let (a;q)_k = ∏_{j=0}^{k−1} (1−aq^j), let (a,b,c;q)_k = (a;q)_k (b;q)_k (c;q)_k, and let Φ_n(q) be the nth cyclotomic polynomial. Prove that for positive integers d and r with gcd(d,r)=1 and r ≤ d, and for every integer n > 1 with n ≡ 1 mod 2d, we have Σ_{k=0}^{n−1} [3dk+r]_q (q^r,q^r,q^d;q^{2d})_k (q^d;q^d)_k^2 q^(k(d−dk−2r)/2) / (q^{2d};q^{2d})_k ≡ [rn]_q q^(r(1−n)/2) mod [n]_q Φ_n(q)^2.

payload.proof_nl:
Let n \equiv 1 \pmod{2d}. By the definition of congruence, there exists an integer t such that
n = 1 + 2dt.

From this representation, n is odd, because it is 1 plus an even integer.

Next, let g be any positive common divisor of d and n. Since g | d, we have g | 2dt, and since g | n as well, it follows that
g \mid (n - 2dt) = 1.
Hence g = 1. Therefore gcd(d,n) = 1.

Also,
r(1-n)/2 = r(1-(1+2dt))/2 = -rdt,
which is an integer. So r(1-n)/2 \in \mathbf{Z}.

Now let k be any integer with 0 \le k \le n. We compute
k(d-dk-2r) = kd - dk^2 - 2kr = -d\,k(k-1) - 2kr.
The product k(k-1) is even, because k and k-1 are consecutive integers. Therefore -d\,k(k-1) is even, and of course -2kr is even. Hence their sum k(d-dk-2r) is even. Dividing by 2, we obtain
k(d-dk-2r)/2 \in \mathbf{Z}.

Thus all the claimed conclusions hold: n is odd, gcd(d,n)=1, r(1-n)/2 is an integer, and for every integer k with 0 \le k \le n one has k(d-dk-2r)/2 \in \mathbf{Z}.

payload.statement_nl: Fix positive integers d and r with gcd(d,r)=1 and r <= d, and let n > 1 satisfy n ≡ 1 mod 2d. Then n is odd, gcd(d,n)=1, the integer r(1-n)/2 is an integer, and for every integer k with 0 <= k <= n one has k(d-dk-2r)/2 ∈ Z.

dependency_assessment.assessment: Only elementary arithmetic and divisibility reasoning are used; no citation issues detected.

detailed_findings.finding: Each conjunct in the lemma statement is proved explicitly from the representation n = 1 + 2dt.
The gcd argument is valid: any positive common divisor g of d and n also divides n - 2dt = 1, hence g = 1.
The parity calculation for k(d-dk-2r)/2 is correct via k(d-dk-2r) = -d k(k-1) - 2kr and evenness of k(k-1).

result_payload.reason: The proof is correct and complete for all stated conclusions. From n ≡ 1 mod 2d it validly writes n = 1 + 2dt, which immediately gives oddness of n and integrality of r(1-n)/2 = -rdt. The argument that any common divisor of d and n must divide 1 correctly proves gcd(d,n)=1. For the final integrality claim, the identity k(d-dk-2r) = -d k(k-1) - 2kr is correct, and both terms are even because k(k-1) is even and 2kr is even, so the half is an integer. The proof matches the lemma sketch and uses only elementary arithmetic with no undeclared or forbidden dependencies.
